column6: Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well, the direct narrative setting behind the commentary's Musa who reaches the water of Midian while seeking a way on his journey.

The verse gives the precise well-side tableau developed beside Qur'an 28:23: Midian's priest has daughters who draw water and fill troughs to water their flock; Exodus says seven where the Qur'anic scene has two.

column5: Moses aids women and waters flock
column6: Exodus makes Moses drive off the hostile shepherds and personally water the flock. It is the close counterpart to the commentary's two women who cannot water until the shepherds leave and are then helped by Musa.
Genesis explicitly calls Joseph's pit empty and waterless. That sharpens the commentary's contrasting Qur'anic well scene, where a caravan's water-drawer lowers a bucket and finds the boy.

Midianite traders draw and lift Joseph from the pit and carry him away. The commentary's Qur'anic caravan likewise removes Joseph from a well, but gives the discovery to a water-carrier lowering his bucket.
When Hagar's water is gone in the wilderness, God opens her eyes to a well. It is a concrete companion to the commentary's traveller whose survival and affairs depend on water being found or brought.
Isaac's servants dig in a valley and find a well described as living water. Its fresh, discovered source closely meets the commentary's deep, full well and its concern for sweet, abundant water.

The verse places three flocks at a well whose mouth is covered by a large stone, because the flocks are watered there. It supplies a biblical well-mouth structure for the commentary's beam, pulley, and watering work.

column5: traveller rolls well stone and waters flock
column6: The travelling Jacob rolls the covering stone from the well's mouth and waters Laban's flock. It joins road, well mechanism, and life-giving water in the way the commentary joins the straight path to the water that sustains a traveller.
Water comes from the struck rock so that the people may drink. This gives a wilderness counterpart to the commentary's claim that water is what keeps communal and travelling life standing.

At Beer, God commands that the people be gathered so that he may give them water. The collective provisioning clarifies why the commentary treats a well as the support of an affair rather than a private possession.

Israel answers the provision of water with the command to the well to spring up and with a song. The liturgical address makes the well itself a source of communal life, matching the commentary's concentrated water imagery.
Seasonal rain makes the land yield produce and trees bear fruit. It directly supplies the rain-to-growing-earth sequence through which the commentary hears the growing Rab and the rain-marked ground.
The promised land drinks water from rain of the heavens, directly holding together sky, rain, ground, and dependence that the commentary develops under the Arabic sky/cloud naming.

The rain in its season yields grain, wine, oil, and grass for livestock. This is a close biblical analogue to the commentary's sequence from poured water to human food, animal provision, and livelihood.
Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rise from the sea before the rain. It is a focused companion to the commentary's cloud that forms above and becomes the bearer of growing water.
The sky turns dark with clouds and wind before a great rain. Its linked weather actors answer the commentary's prolonged cloud and moist south-wind scene without requiring the same wind direction.
Job describes God drawing up drops of water and distilling them as rain. It offers a precise account of the water-to-cloud-to-rain process behind the commentary's layered, plant-growing cloud.
The skies pour water down abundantly on humankind. This gives a direct counterpart to the commentary's gathering of abundant water and rain as public benefit.
The thick cloud is loaded with moisture and then spread abroad. Its particular image of a moisture-bearing cloud parallels the commentary's layered cloud and the wet wind associated with it.

column5: tree by water, leaf does not wither
column6: The tree planted by channels of water bears fruit and does not wither. It is the closest biblical image for the commentary's tender plant that remains fresh even through summer.

column5: green pasture and waters of rest
column6: The shepherd makes the speaker rest in green pastures and leads beside waters of rest. It combines the commentary's growing ground, water, guidance, and wayfarer in one pastoral line.
God waters furrows, softens earth with showers, and blesses its growth. This particularly matches the commentary's first rain writing vegetation into the ground and the cloud that grows plants.
God waters the mountains from his upper chambers, and the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his work. It is a close scriptural formulation of heavenly water sustaining terrestrial growth.

column5: grass and plants grow from water
column6: The same hymn says God causes grass to grow for cattle and plants for human cultivation. It supplies the food-and-livestock outcome that the commentary connects to rain and provision.

column5: desert turned to pools and springs
column6: God turns desert into a pool and parched ground into water springs. The reversal makes a concrete companion to rain repairing a people's condition and to water being drawn from otherwise dry ground.
God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on hills. Its exact three-part image is especially close to the commentary's cloud, rain, and plant meeting.

column5: rain for seed, rich bread, livestock
column6: Rain is given for the seed sown in the ground, producing abundant bread and pasture for livestock. This directly meets the commentary's water, food, animals, and sustaining livelihood.

column5: waters in wilderness, streams in desert
column6: Waters break out in the wilderness and streams in the desert. The verse makes the life-restoring turn from dryness to water that the commentary associates with rain, mercy, and fresh life.

column5: rivers, fountains, pools on dry land
column6: God opens rivers and fountains and turns wilderness into pools and dry ground into springs. This is a direct biblical counterpart to both the commentary's well-water and its fear that water may sink out of reach.

Water is poured on thirsty land and streams on dry ground. It directly parallels the commentary's rain sent to barren earth, while its following spiritual application makes the literal image more than a weather report.

The compassionate guide leads the hungry and thirsty to springs of water. Its explicit joining of guidance, a way, and water is a strong companion to the commentary's straight path beside the sustaining well.

God continually guides, satisfies the parched person, and makes that person like a watered garden and an unfailing spring. It closely joins the commentary's guidance, fresh life, and never-failing water.

column5: tree by water stays green in drought
column6: The water-side tree has green leaves and does not cease bearing fruit in drought. Its drought-resistant freshness is a particularly close counterpart to the commentary's summer-unwithered ribbe plant.

God leads the returning people to watercourses on a straight path where they do not stumble. This is an unusually exact meeting of the commentary's dosdoğru yol with water that makes the journey possible.

Where the temple river goes, every living creature lives and the water becomes fresh. It supplies a concentrated account of water's restorative, life-making work behind the commentary's full, sweet, beneficial water.

Trees beside the river bear fruit continually and their leaves do not wither because their water comes from the sanctuary. It directly amplifies the commentary's enduring green plant and abundant sustaining water.
The rain is given in its proper season, including the early and latter rains. It provides a biblical seasonal setting for the commentary's first rain that marks the earth with vegetation.

column5: spring rain, storm clouds, field plants
column6: God makes storm clouds, gives rain showers, and provides vegetation in every field. The verse has the same cloud-rain-plant sequence developed in the commentary.

column5: living waters in summer and winter
column6: Living waters flow in both summer and winter. Its year-round flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's fresh plant that does not fade in summer and its well of plentiful water.
The Father sends rain on both just and unjust. It gives a New Testament articulation of rain as unearned divine beneficence, relevant to the commentary's rain as mercy and benefit.

column5: weary traveller seated at Jacob's well
column6: Jesus, wearied by travel, sits at Jacob's well. This makes a close well-side counterpart to the commentary's traveller who reaches water and whose journey depends on it.
A woman arrives to draw water, turning the well into a meeting between a traveller and a woman obtaining water. It closely accompanies the commentary's Musa, the two women, and the Midian water.

column5: gift of God and living water
column6: Jesus offers living water at the well. It moves the commentary's full, beneficial well from physical support to a divine gift without erasing the scene of drawing water.
The water Jesus gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. Its self-renewing spring is a concentrated Christian analogue to the commentary's water that keeps life and affairs standing.

The believer is described as the source from whom streams of living water flow. It extends the living-water image from the well to an overflowing source, a useful counterpart to the commentary's abundant gathered water.
God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness. It exactly connects divine rain with the food and livelihood results developed in the commentary.
Paul plants, Apollos waters, and God gives the growth. Its agricultural distinction makes explicit the commentary's basic figure: water serves growth, yet the giver of growth remains God.
Israel's wilderness journey takes place under the cloud. Together with the water in verse 4, this creates a Christian rereading in which cloud and water accompany a people on the way.

column5: water from the rock for the journey
column6: The wilderness people drink from the spiritual rock that follows them. It is a strong counterpart to the commentary's claim that water beside the traveller sustains the journey and its affairs.

column5: land drinks rain and yields plants
column6: Land that drinks repeatedly falling rain and produces useful vegetation receives blessing. It directly restates the commentary's heavenly water making the earth grow.

column5: farmer waits for early and late rain
column6: The farmer waits for the earth's precious fruit through the early and late rains. It offers a New Testament seasonal analogue to the commentary's first rain and rain-grown vegetation.

Jude's false teachers are waterless clouds carried by winds. This is a deliberate negative inversion of the commentary's moist, rain-bearing cloud that grows plants: a cloud that promises but gives no life.

column5: springs without water and driven mist
column6: The false teachers are compared to waterless springs and mists driven by storm. Its paired failures of well and cloud form a precise inverse to the commentary's full well and productive cloud.
The Lamb shepherds and guides the thirsty to springs of the water of life. It closely meets the commentary's way, guidance, shepherding provision, and water that removes want.
The thirsty receive water of life freely from the spring. It gives an eschatological form to the commentary's water as indispensable gift and remedy for need.

A bright river of water of life proceeds from God's throne. The throne-source relationship gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's unusual claim that water is a kingdom's or traveller's holding power.

The trees beside the life-river bear fruit continually and their leaves serve healing. Its flourishing trees supply a Christian counterpart to the commentary's plant nourished into unfading freshness.

A water source rising from the earth waters the whole ground before rain is mentioned. Because the Hebrew term's exact physical sense is debated, it is a cautious companion to the commentary's two routes of water: sky-rain and water drawn from below.

column5: camels at well at drawing time
column6: Abraham's servant stops with camels at a well at the time women come to draw water. It supplies the practical journey-and-well setting behind the commentary's water carried by a traveller.
Rebekah draws until the camels have drunk. Her labour at the well gives another concrete biblical instance of water as the support of travellers and animals.

The waters at Marah are made sweet so the people can drink. It offers a specific biblical analogue to the commentary's distinction of abundant water that can be called sweet and water that repairs a people's condition.

The good land is defined by brooks, fountains, and depths issuing in valley and hill. It complements the commentary's deep water-filled well and its concern that a water source might withdraw underground.
Joyful drawing from wells becomes the image of salvation. The verse gives a scriptural way in which the literal action central to the commentary's pulley and well bears a second, saving sense.

column5: needy seek water and find none
column6: The poor and needy seek water with their tongues parched, and God answers them. It is a direct companion to the commentary's question of who can bring water when a community's water has gone down.

The heavens rain and the earth opens to sprout salvation and righteousness. It recasts the commentary's rain-and-growing-earth image as an ethical and saving figure rather than a purely agricultural one.
The thirsty are invited to come to water without payment. Its invitation turns the commentary's traveller's necessary water into a public gift available to those in need.

The people abandon a fountain of living water for cracked cisterns that cannot retain water. It offers a negative well-and-storage counterpart to the commentary's gathered water and the structural devices at a well's mouth.

The commentary's source label س م و develops sky, cloud, rain, and plant under samāʾ. Hebrew šāmayim in this verse is a cognate sky term, but the verse keeps heaven and its rain distinct while making the land drink the rain; that difference is informative rather than evidence for identical usage.

The commentary explicitly ties أَنْعَمْتَ and n-ʿ-m to freshness and beneficent support. Hebrew neʿimot, a cognate form here, accompanies the path of life and enduring delight; it gives a linguistic and contextual companion to the commentary's path plus life-giving blessing.

column5: Arabic q-w-m and Hebrew qwm restore
column6: The commentary's ق و م label names the pulley and what makes an affair stand. Hebrew qwm in this verse describes raising up and restoring enduring foundations; beside the watered-garden guidance of verse 11, it supplies a cognate support-and-restoration sense without claiming a well in Isaiah 58:12.

The Mishnah lists Miriam's well among things prepared at creation's twilight. This later Jewish tradition makes a well a providential provision for Israel, clarifying the commentary's water as what sustains a travelling community.

column5: clouds of glory and Miriam's well
column6: The Talmud associates Israel's wilderness gifts with the cloud and Miriam's well. Its deliberate pairing is an especially close Jewish counterpart to this section's meeting of growing cloud and well.

On Genesis 37:24, the Talmud reads "no water" as leaving room for snakes and scorpions. The interpretation sharpens the commentary's Joseph contrast: the biblical pit is not a usable water source even when it is not simply empty space.

The common division of Genesis Rabbah says that the water rose to meet Jacob at Haran. That interpretive expansion transforms the covered well of Genesis 29 into a responsive source, useful beside the commentary's well apparatus and abundant water.

The tradition commonly cited at this place has the well water rise for Rebekah as she draws for the camels. It re-reads the traveller-and-well service of Genesis 24 as a sign of blessing, adding a Jewish interpretive layer to the commentary's water as benefit.

The Mishnah fixes when a community begins mentioning and requesting rain. Its concrete liturgical ordering of rain gives a Jewish communal counterpart to the commentary's rain as mercy and repair rather than merely weather.

The Talmud develops the scriptural comparison of Torah with water. This changes water from material provision into descending and sought instruction, a useful interpretive bridge to the commentary's pairing of guidance with sustaining water.
On a wilderness road the Ethiopian traveller sees water and asks for baptism. The scene is a Christian travel-and-water meeting that gives the commentary's road beside water a ritual extension.
Human flesh is compared to grass that withers and a flower that falls. As an explicit inverse, it helps define the significance of the commentary's exceptional plant that does not wither in summer.

The Didache prefers baptism in living water. Its ritual preference turns running or fresh water into a sign of new life, extending the commentary's literal contrast between a life-giving source and lost water.

In the usual chapter division, Mary goes out with a water jar and hears the annunciatory greeting. This Christian apocryphal well-side encounter belongs beside the commentary's women at water, where drawing water becomes a setting for divine gift.

column4: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 15
column6: Augustine's treatment of the Samaritan-woman scene reads Christ's living water as spiritual grace rather than ordinary well water alone. It shows how a Christian interpreter changes the literal traveller-and-well meeting that parallels the commentary.

Origen's homily on Isaac's reopened wells treats digging wells as recovering the deep waters of Scripture. The reading gives a Christian interpretive afterlife to the commentary's well as a source that must be reached and kept open.

The waters below the sky are gathered into one place so that dry ground appears. It is a foundational counterpart to the commentary's claim that abundant water is named for its gathering and to its distinction between water above and water held below.

Israel reaches Elim, with twelve water springs and seventy palms, and camps by the water. This joins a travelling people, a water source, and flourishing vegetation in the concrete way the commentary joins road, well, and growing ground.

Israel asks to travel on the king's highway while promising not to drink from field, vineyard, or well. The verse unusually binds road, traveller, well water, and king in one practical scene, directly meeting the commentary's straight path and water-as-royal-support imagery.

column5: well dug by nobles with staffs
column6: The well is dug by princes and hollowed by nobles with their staffs. As the necessary continuation of the well-song, it makes rulership and a constructed water source meet, closely accompanying the commentary's waters called rulers and its beam-and-pulley well mouth.

David longs for water from the well by Bethlehem's gate. The king's desire for a particular well makes water a royal concern, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary's phrase that a community's waters are its kings.

column5: men draw and carry well water to David
column6: David's warriors break through, draw water from the Bethlehem well, and bring it to him. The verse supplies the physical act of drawing and carrying water for a ruler, beside the commentary's pulley, traveller's water, and royal-water wordplay.

Elisha throws salt into a spring and declares its waters healed, so that death and barrenness will no longer come from it. It gives a sharp biblical counterpart to rain or water improving a people's condition and to the commentary's fresh, beneficial water.

The valley will be filled with water even though neither wind nor rain is seen. Its explicit separation of water provision from visible wind and rain is a useful contrary configuration beside the commentary's wind moving cloud toward rain.

The verse calls YHWH melekh, a cognate of the commentary's م ل ك / mālik label, while placing him over the flood. It gives a substantive Hebrew king-and-water meeting, not merely a shared root, beside the commentary's water as what holds an affair together.

column5: Baca valley made a spring by rain
column6: Those crossing the Valley of Baca make it a place of springs, and early rain covers it with blessings. The transforming rain-and-spring image supplies a pilgrimage-scale companion to the commentary's path that cannot be separated from water.

column5: full clouds empty rain on earth
column6: When clouds are full, they pour rain on the earth. The compact image answers the commentary's layered cloud, its accumulated moisture, and the eventual transfer of gathered water to the ground.

By divine knowledge the depths break open and the skies drip dew. It is a compact biblical pairing of water from below with moisture from above, closely matching the commentary's well-water and heaven-rain as two routes of water.

A person who boasts of a false gift is like clouds and wind with no rain. This negative weather image precisely defines the loss implicit in the commentary's productive cloud: visible cloud and wind do not suffice unless water reaches the earth.

column5: garden fountain and well of living water
column6: The beloved is called a garden fountain, a well of living waters, and streams flowing from Lebanon. Its gathered garden, well, freshness, and flow make it a particularly close biblical companion to the commentary's full well and unfading vegetation.
YHWH guards the vineyard and waters it continually. It supplies the direct divine-cultivator sense that the commentary hears in Rab as the one associated with plant growth.

column5: sowing by waters with ox and donkey
column6: The blessed sow beside all waters and let ox and donkey range out. It joins water, cultivation, and working animals, the same practical provision sequence that the commentary traces from rain to food and livestock.

The nobles send servants for water, but cisterns have none and the vessels return empty. Its social consequence of missing water is a direct counterpart to the commentary's question of who can bring water when a community's source has withdrawn.

Jeremiah asks whether foreign gods or the heavens can give showers, and confesses that YHWH made all these things. This makes rain a dependent gift of the creator, closely matching the commentary's rain as mercy and benefit rather than autonomous weather.

The restored people receive grain, wine, oil, flock, and herd, and their life becomes like a watered garden. This is the necessary agricultural continuation of the watercourse-and-straight-way image in Jeremiah 31:9 already relevant to the commentary.
God's coming is compared to rain and to the latter rain watering the earth. It directly supplies the rain-as-divine-mercy reading that the commentary develops around rahmet and revived ground.
God will be like dew to Israel, and Israel will blossom like the lily. This adds the secondary, non-rain moisture route by which divine beneficence makes a plant fresh and flourishing.

column5: shut sky so rain does not fall
column6: The witnesses have authority to shut the sky so that rain does not fall during their prophecy. Its withheld-rain image is a specific inverse to the commentary's cloud and rain as mercy that restores life.

The earth is commanded to sprout grass, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees. Read after the gathered-water scene of Genesis 1:9, its own contribution is the created vegetation that corresponds to the commentary's ground marked and grown green.

column5: cistern and own well as ethical figure
column6: The proverb commands drinking from one's own cistern and well. It takes the literal infrastructure central to the commentary and makes its contained water an ethical image of faithful, rightly bounded household life.

column5: Adam recognizes need of rain and prays
column6: In the usual division, the midrash explains the delayed rain of Genesis 2 by saying that rain came after Adam recognized its need and prayed. It adds a Jewish reading in which rain, vegetation, human need, and prayer are deliberately joined.

column5: well enclosures for pilgrims and animals
column6: The Mishnah permits a distinctive post-and-enclosure arrangement around wells so that festival travellers' animals can be watered. Its legal concern with well-side construction, travellers, and animal water is unusually close to the commentary's detailed well-mouth apparatus.

The Honi story treats drought-ending rain as a communal need and distinguishes an unhelpful rain from the desired beneficial rain. It gives a Jewish narrative counterpart to the commentary's rain that repairs a people's condition.

The sick man says that when the pool's water is stirred, he has no one to put him in it before another enters. It supplies a Christian scene where need, water, and the absence of a helper meet, a useful counterpart to the women who cannot water without aid.

column5: leading ox or donkey to water
column6: Jesus invokes the ordinary act of untying an ox or donkey and leading it to water. The concrete animal-watering practice complements the commentary's water as livelihood and its well scene of flocks needing to be watered.

The waters become bitter and people die from them. This is a specific negative counterpart to the commentary's sweet, abundant, life-sustaining water and to its image of water repairing rather than harming a community.

Hermas's vision of the Church as a tower built on water explains water as the means through which life is saved. This early Christian interpretation turns water into an actual foundation, closely echoing the commentary's qiwām and milāk language for what keeps a matter standing.
